Projections

What the violet years mean

After the last measured year, the timeline continues to 2050 in violet. Those values are statistical extrapolations from each grid cell’s own recent record. They are not climate-model output: they do not know emissions, physics, or hard limits (for example sea ice reaching zero).

Each cell and layer is projected on its own from the most recent complete 30-year window. Monthly and seasonal maps repeat the same construction for that month or season. Cells missing any year in that window stay gray. The 30-year trend map has no projected years.

Trend fit

Write the window values as \(y_i\) for \(i = 0,\ldots,29\), centered time \(x_i = i - \bar{x}\) with \(\bar{x} = 14.5\), and window mean \(\bar{y}\). The ordinary least-squares slope is

$$ b = \frac{\sum_{i=0}^{29} x_i\,(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sum_{i=0}^{29} x_i^2},\qquad \sum_{i=0}^{29} x_i^2 = \frac{30(30^2-1)}{12} = 2247.5. $$

Residual standard deviation (28 degrees of freedom) and the slope’s \(t\) statistic are

$$ s = \sqrt{\frac{1}{28}\sum_{i=0}^{29}\bigl(y_i - \bar{y} - b x_i\bigr)^2},\qquad t = \frac{b}{s\big/\sqrt{\sum x_i^2}}. $$

Damped central estimate

Weak trends relative to year-to-year noise should not be projected at full strength. The atlas uses the James–Stein-style weight

$$ w = \begin{cases} 1 - \dfrac{1}{t^2} & \text{if } |t| > 1,\\[0.6em] 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases} $$

A step \(h\) years after the window midpoint (\(h = 14.5 + k + 1\) for the \(k\)-th future year, \(k = 0,1,\ldots\)) has central estimate

$$ \hat{y}(h) = \bar{y} + w\,b\,h. $$

If \(|t|\le 1\), the projection collapses to the recent mean. Temperature layers usually keep \(w\) near 1; noisy fields often shrink toward 0.

95% range

The location chart shows a classical Student-\(t\) prediction interval for one future observation, widened by a fixed factor \(c = 1.4\) after a hindcast found the textbook band too narrow:

$$ \hat{y}(h) \;\pm\; c\,t_{0.975,\,28}\,s\,\sqrt{1 + \frac{1}{30} + \frac{h^2}{\sum x_i^2}}, \qquad t_{0.975,\,28} \approx 2.048. $$

The band grows with lead time \(h\). It still omits structural breaks, changing slopes, and dataset inhomogeneity, so treat it as a lower bound on real uncertainty.

One possible year on the map

Real years do not sit on a line. For calendar year \(Y\), the map adds the residual of one past window year

$$ j = \bigl(Y\cdot 2654435761\bigr) \bmod 30,\qquad \tilde{y}(h) = \hat{y}(h) + \bigl(y_j - \bar{y} - b x_j\bigr). $$

The same \(j\) is used for every cell in that year, so spatial warm/cool patterns stay coherent. That map field is one plausible year under the fitted noise, not a forecast of that exact year. The side panel’s central value and range use \(\hat{y}(h)\), not \(\tilde{y}(h)\).

Hindcast check

To measure error, each layer was fit on 30 years ending 25 years before the latest observed year, then projected forward and compared with measurements. “Typical miss” is the median absolute gap between \(\hat{y}\) and the measured value across cells. The no-change column is the miss from holding each cell at its 30-year mean. Bold marks the better method.

Temperature layers beat a no-change guess (roughly \(0.5^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) typical miss 16–25 years out for surface temperature). Pressure, wind, cloud, moisture, sea ice, and energy layers usually do not—treat their violet years as variability sketches, not a direction of travel. Before widening, the textbook 95% interval held only about 87% of measured values; with \(c = 1.4\) it held 93–98% by layer.

Limits

One hindcast window is thin evidence, and reanalysis layers can contain observing-system changes that look like trends. A straight line cannot bend: if warming accelerates or slows, \(\hat{y}\) will miss, and the interval does not include that possibility. For decisions that matter, use published climate-model projections such as those assessed by the IPCC. Table numbers were computed from the atlas grids in November 2026 and will shift slightly when the data update.
